  coordinator, replacing Matt Nagy. But Andy Reid has called Kansas City's plays for almost all of his tenure
  (the exception was the last weeks of 2017, when he handed them to Nagy), including throughout Bieniemy's
  first stint (2018-2022), and said in January 2026 that play-calling remains his job. The
  bigger Chiefs change is a player: they signed Kenneth Walker III, the Super Bowl LX MVP, from Seattle in
  March.[^reid]

Here is what the first four weeks of 2026 show.

```{python}
#| label: fig-coord-card
#| fig-cap: "Coordinator-change usage cards: 2025 (grey) against 2026 Weeks 1-4 (blue, with a bar showing about ±2 standard errors of sampling noise), and the new play-caller's previous team in 2025 (gold diamond) where there is one. Where a grey ring shows around a blue dot, nothing moved (Kansas City's tight-end share). Top row: neutral-situation PROE, in percentage points. Bottom row: how the offense plays, as percentages: motion (any motion before or at the snap, FTN definition), play-action (share of passes), under center (share of plays), and the share of targets that went to running backs and to tight ends. Read across a card: where the blue dot has moved toward the gold diamond, the new play-caller's habit has arrived; a move smaller than the bar is not yet evidence. Data: nflverse play-by-play and FTN charting; regular seasons."
CARDS = [("DET", "Detroit Lions", "2025: Morton, then Campbell", "2026: Drew Petzing", "ARI", "Petzing's 2025 Cardinals"),
         ("LAC", "Los Angeles Chargers", "2025: Greg Roman", "2026: Mike McDaniel", "MIA", "McDaniel's 2025 Dolphins"),
         ("KC", "Kansas City Chiefs", "2025: Reid calls (Nagy OC)", "2026: Reid calls (Bieniemy OC)", None, None)]
RATES = [("motion", "Motion"), ("play_action", "Play-action"), ("under_center", "Under center"),
         ("rb_tgt", "RB target share"), ("te_tgt", "TE target share")]
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(6.6, 5.8))
gsp = fig.add_gridspec(3, 3, height_ratios=[0.42, 0.55, 2.2], hspace=0.42, wspace=0.12)
for c, (tm, full, before, after, prev, prev_lab) in enumerate(CARDS):
    a25, a26 = TEAMS.loc[(2025, tm)], TEAMS.loc[(2026, tm)]
    pv = TEAMS.loc[(2025, prev)] if prev else None
    hd = fig.add_subplot(gsp[0, c])
    hd.axis("off")
    hd.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((0.01, 0.02), 0.98, 0.96, boxstyle="round,pad=0.0,rounding_size=0.06",
                                transform=hd.transAxes, fc=style.OFFENSE_TINT, ec="none"))
    hd.text(0.5, 0.72, full, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8.2, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK, transform=hd.transAxes)
    hd.text(0.5, 0.42, before, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.4, color=style.INK_2, transform=hd.transAxes)
    hd.text(0.5, 0.17, after, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.4, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontweight="bold",
            transform=hd.transAxes)
    # PROE strip
    ax = fig.add_subplot(gsp[1, c])
    ax.set_xlim(-15, 10)
    ax.set_ylim(-0.6, 0.6)
    ax.axvline(0, color=GREY, lw=0.7)
    se = 2 * a26.proe_se
    ax.plot([a26.proe - se, a26.proe + se], [0, 0], color=style.OFFENSE, lw=4, alpha=0.25, solid_capstyle="round")
    ax.scatter([a25.proe], [0], s=58, color=GREY, zorder=3)
    ax.scatter([a26.proe], [0], s=30, color=style.OFFENSE, zorder=4)
    if pv is not None:
        ax.scatter([pv.proe], [0], s=40, marker="D", color=TE_RING, edgecolor=style.INK_2, lw=0.5, zorder=3)
    ax.set_yticks([0])
    ax.set_yticklabels(["PROE" if c == 0 else ""], fontsize=7)
    ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=6.5)
    ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
    ax.set_xticks([-10, 0, 10])
    ax.set_xlabel("neutral PROE (percentage points)", fontsize=6.5, labelpad=1)
    # rates
    ax = fig.add_subplot(gsp[2, c])
    for i, (k, lab) in enumerate(RATES):
        y = len(RATES) - 1 - i
        n = a26.n_targets if k.endswith("tgt") else (a26.n_pass if k == "play_action" else a26.n_plays)
        p = a26[k] / 100
        se = 200 * np.sqrt(max(p * (1 - p), 1e-6) / n)
        ax.plot([a26[k] - se, a26[k] + se], [y, y], color=style.OFFENSE, lw=4, alpha=0.25, solid_capstyle="round")
        ax.plot([a25[k], a26[k]], [y, y], color=GREY, lw=0.8, zorder=2)
        ax.scatter([a25[k]], [y], s=52, color=GREY, zorder=3)
        ax.scatter([a26[k]], [y], s=26, color=style.OFFENSE, zorder=4)
        if pv is not None:
            ax.scatter([pv[k]], [y], s=34, marker="D", color=TE_RING, edgecolor=style.INK_2, lw=0.5, zorder=3)
    ax.set_yticks(range(len(RATES)))
    ax.set_yticklabels([lab for _, lab in RATES][::-1] if c == 0 else [], fontsize=7)
    ax.set_xlim(0, 85)
    ax.set_xticks([0, 20, 40, 60, 80])
    ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=6.5)
    ax.set_xlabel("% of plays, passes or targets", fontsize=6.5, labelpad=1)
    ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
    if prev_lab:
        ax.text(0.98, -0.2, f"◆ {prev_lab}", transform=ax.transAxes, ha="right", fontsize=6.2, color=style.INK_2)
fig.legend(handles=[Line2D([], [], marker="o", ls="", color=GREY, label="2025, full season"),
                    Line2D([], [], marker="o", ls="", color=style.OFFENSE, label="2026, Weeks 1-4"),
                    Line2D([], [], marker="D", ls="", color=TE_RING, mec=style.INK_2, label="New play-caller's 2025 team")],
           loc="lower center", ncol=3, fontsize=7, bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.06))
plt.show()
```

Read the three cards one at a time, the way you would read a scouting report.

**Los Angeles: the fingerprint arrived on day one.** The Chargers used motion on 52% of their plays in 2025
under Roman. Through four games under McDaniel, the rate is 72%, almost exactly what his last Miami offense
did (71%), and the jump is far outside the noise bar. The offense has also leaned hard on the run: a neutral PROE of about
−10 after +2 in 2025. McDaniel's habit and Harbaugh's identity point the same way here (McDaniel's 2025 Dolphins
were about −5), so don't credit the coordinator alone, and the PROE is noisier than the motion rate.

The fantasy lesson is in the targets, and it runs *against* McDaniel's fingerprint. His Miami offenses
concentrated the ball on two receivers. Through four weeks in Los Angeles no Charger has drawn even 18% of the
targets: second-year receiver Tre Harris leads at about 18%, while Ladd McConkey, who drew about 21% in the 2025
games he played, is down to about 15%, the clearest loser so far. The backs' share of the targets rose too.
When a play-caller who funnels targets spreads them, the likeliest reason is the roster (he hasn't found his
Hill yet), not a new philosophy. The likelier bet is that the shares consolidate on whichever receiver he can
feature with motion and manufactured touches, but four weeks can't say which; and in a run-first offense even
the winner's volume is capped. The clearer beneficiary is the lead back, Omarion Hampton, who took 52% of the
Chargers' runs.

**Detroit: a fingerprint plus a roster move.** The Lions' tight end target share went from 17% to 23%, toward
Petzing's Arizona level, and Sam LaPorta drew about 20% of the targets. Play-action rose from 25% to 31%, and
motion fell from 60% to 51%, toward the 44% of Petzing's last Cardinals offense. Each move is about the size of
the noise bar, so they are hints rather than proof. And not everything moved his way: Detroit is still under
center on about 46% of its plays (48% in 2025), nowhere near Arizona's 28%. Petzing has kept that piece of the
offense he inherited, which is a reminder that a play-caller adapts to his line and his quarterback too.

Be honest about the tight end number as well. Arizona's third of the targets was partly scheme and partly
that Trey McBride was simply the Cardinals' best receiver for three years; the scheme part travels to Detroit,
the McBride part doesn't. And LaPorta drew about 19% of the targets in the nine 2025 games he played, so much
of the team's rise is just a healthy LaPorta, not a new philosophy. (The 2025 "before" dots also mix two
play-callers, Morton and then Campbell.) Who gives up the targets? So far, slightly, both receivers: Amon-Ra
St. Brown from 31% to 29% and Jameson Williams from 19% to 16%, moves inside the noise for now, but the
direction the fingerprint predicts.

The PROE jump (−6 to about 0) is harder to read. It isn't the score: the Lions trailed on an average snap
by about four points, but PROE is measured only in neutral situations, where they were roughly level, and
xpass already allows for the score. It is about one and a half noise bars, so it is a lean, pointing toward
Petzing's pass-first Arizona (+6), not proof. The clearest change is not scheme at all: with Montgomery traded,
Gibbs took 83% of Detroit's runs, up from 56%. That is a usage change you could have predicted in March.

**Kansas City: same play-caller, different ingredients.** Reid still calls the plays, so the theory says
little should change, and the PROE barely did. But the Chiefs have been under center on 39% of plays (19% in
2025) and have used play-action on 37% of passes (15% in 2025), both far outside the noise. That pattern fits a
team built around a new lead back, Walker, who took 76% of the Chiefs' runs (and about 16% of the targets). It
may also be Bieniemy: a coordinator who doesn't call plays still builds the weekly game plan, the run-game
install and the situational packages, and four games can't separate his influence from Walker's. Either way the
lesson is the first step of the method: when the play-caller hasn't changed, look for the roster change and the
game plan, not a new fingerprint.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"Four weeks in, the new offense is clearly X." Four games are about 240-260 plays and 120-180
neutral-situation plays per team. With that many plays, a team's PROE has a standard error of about 4 percentage points, so a
change of 5 or 6 points can be noise. Rates measured on every play (motion, under center) settle faster than
rates measured on a subset (PROE, target shares). Big, consistent moves toward the new play-caller's old
numbers (the Chargers' motion rate) are believable early; small moves, or moves against the fingerprint, need
another month.

The same goes for a player's own shares. In 2025, a receiver's or tight end's target share over Weeks 1-4
correlated about 0.67 with his share over the rest of the season, and the typical miss was about 5 percentage
points: enough to tell a 30% alpha from a 15% third option, not enough to tell 22% from 26%.[^inseason]
:::

## Watch for it on Sunday

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it on Sunday: the scheme-shift draft"}
Before the season (or now, for the 2026 test cases), pick one team with a new play-caller and write down a
prediction for each skill position. Then check it after four weeks and again at mid-season.

**Before kickoff (the forecast):**

- **Who calls the plays?** If it's the same person as last year, look for roster changes instead.
- **His last offense's fingerprint:** neutral PROE, plays per game, motion and play-action rates, and the
  share of targets to RBs, TEs and WRs. Which way does each differ from this team's last season?
- **Translate it:** which position's share should rise, which should fall, and does the team's total
  volume rise or fall? Name the player who gains most and the one who loses most.

**During the game (the live check):**

- **Who's on the field on third down and in the two-minute drill?** That's the passing-down back and the
  receivers the play-caller trusts.
- **Does the tight end release or stay in?** Count it for one quarter: on how many dropbacks did he run a
  route?
- **Who's in at the goal line?** Watch the substitution inside the 5. That player owns the touchdowns.
- **What's the score?** Discount the usage from a blowout: the leading team's carries and the trailing team's
  targets are game script, not role.
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 1: first-and-goal at the 2"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-goal
#| fig-cap: "First-and-goal at the 2, third quarter, score tied (illustrative). The offense is in 22 personnel from the I-formation: two tight ends attached to the line (Y and U, gold rings), the quarterback under center, a fullback (F, gold ring) and a tailback, G (green ring), stacked behind him, and one receiver, X. The team's lead back, who has played most of the snaps today, jogged off as this group came on; G is the backup. The defense has answered with its goal-line package, nearly all of it within four yards of the line."
off = line5() + [O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0, "Q"), O("FB", "FB", -4.4, 0, "F"), O("G", "RB", -6.8, 0, "G"),
                 O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"), O("U", "TE", -0.7, -4.8, "U"), O("X", "WR", -1.5, -10.5, "X")]
dfn = [D("E1", "DE", 0.8, -6.2, "E"), D("T1", "DT", 0.8, -2.4, "T"), D("N", "DT", 0.8, -0.8, "T"),
       D("T2", "DT", 0.8, 0.8, "T"), D("T3", "DT", 0.8, 2.4, "T"), D("E2", "DE", 0.8, 6.2, "E"),
       D("L1", "MIKE", 2.8, -2.2, "M"), D("L2", "MIKE", 2.8, 2.2, "M"), D("L3", "SAM", 1.4, 7.8, "S"),
       D("C1", "CB", 1.2, -10.5, "C"), D("S1", "SS", 3.6, 0.0, "SS")]
pg = Play(off, dfn, los=108, to_go=2)
pg.highlight("Y", "U", "FB", color=TE_RING)
pg.highlight("G", color=WATCH)
fld = pg.draw(lateral=(-14.5, 14.5), window=(-9.5, 6.0), title=False)
no_numbers(fld.ax)
say(fld, pg, "goal line", (2.9, 10.6), fs=6.5, color=style.INK_2)
say(fld, pg, "lead back: on the sideline\nG, the backup, came in", (-6.0, 8.0), fs=6.3, color=style.INK_2)
plt.show()
```

**Who is the likely ball carrier? And what does this substitution tell a fantasy manager who owns the lead
back, or is thinking of picking up G?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**A run, most likely to G behind the fullback.** Two tight ends attached, a fullback, the quarterback under
center and one receiver add up to a run-first goal-line call: a lead play or power with F leading through the
hole. Play-action to a tight end is the main alternative, which is why goal-line defenses still keep a
safety and a corner on their heels. A quarterback sneak is possible, but at the 2 rather than the 1 it is a
less natural call for most teams.

The usage lesson is the substitution, not the play. The coaches took their lead back off the field at the 2.
If they do it every time they get close, G owns the goal-line role, and the touchdowns go with it: the Seattle
pattern from earlier in the chapter, where the back with fewer carries scored more than twice as many
rushing touchdowns. For the lead back's manager it caps his touchdown total, however many yards he gains
between the 20s. For G, it is the opening's "14 snaps, two touchdowns" backup, and the question to answer
before picking him up is whether this happens every week. Watch the next few trips inside the 5. If it is G
every time, he is a touchdown-dependent but real option in standard scoring, and less of one in PPR unless he also
catches passes. Had this been the 1-yard line for a team with a tush-push quarterback, the answer would
change again: the quarterback takes the ball, as Philadelphia's did in the film room.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 2: the receiver who changes teams"}
A wide receiver drew 25% of his old team's targets as its clear number one. That team ran 64 plays a game and
dropped back to pass on 62% of them. He signs with a team whose new play-caller's last offense ran 58 plays a
game and dropped back on 54%. On both teams about 87% of dropbacks end in a target (the rest are sacks,
scrambles and throwaways). The new play-caller's offenses have also thrown about 30% of their targets to tight
ends, against 18% on the receiver's old team, and the new team has a good tight end.

**Use the volume equation: roughly how many targets per game should you forecast for him, before and after the
move? What in the new offense could cut his share, and what would make you raise the forecast during the
season?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**About 7 a game, down from about 8.6.** Work the equation one term at a time. Old team: 64 plays × 0.62 pass
rate × 0.87 target rate ≈ 34.5 team targets a game, and 25% of that is about 8.6. New team: 58 × 0.54 × 0.87 ≈
27.2 team targets, and 25% of that is about 6.8. Same player, same share, about a fifth fewer targets: roughly
30 over a 17-game season, and at a typical two-thirds catch rate about 20 fewer catches (20 PPR points) before
you count a single lost yard.

The share is the term to argue about. His 25% is his role as a clear number one, and that part tends to travel.
But the new play-caller's position split sends about 30% of the targets to tight ends instead of 18%. Those 12
extra points of share come from somewhere, usually the second and third receivers first, but a number one can
lose a couple of points too. A forecast of 22-25% (6-7 targets a game) is the honest range.

Raise it if, after a month, his share is clearly above that range (28-30%, beyond the typical 5-point early
miss), meaning the play-caller is building around him more than his history suggests; if the team throws more
than its play-caller's history (a higher PROE, or more snaps from a faster pace); or if the tight end gets hurt.
Be careful with extra passing that comes from trailing: that is game script, not taste, and it won't hold in the
weeks the team keeps it close.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 3: third-and-8, down 10 in the fourth"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-third
#| fig-cap: "Third-and-8, fourth quarter, the offense trailing by 10. 11 personnel in trips: three receivers to the right (Z wide, H and the tight end Y, gold ring, detached into the slots) and X alone on the left, the quarterback in the shotgun and a running back (B, green ring) beside him. This team has two backs: A, its early-down runner, who had 18 carries and 1 catch in the first three quarters, and B. The defense is in dime: six defensive backs ($ the nickel, D the sixth), two safeties deep and only five men in the box."
off = line5() + [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.2, -2.1, "B"),
                 O("X", "WR", -0.7, -15.0, "X"), O("Y", "TE", -1.5, 8.0, "Y"),
                 O("H", "WR", -1.5, 11.5, "H"), O("Z", "WR", -0.7, 17.0, "Z")]
dfn = [D("E1", "DE", 1.0, -5.5, "E"), D("T1", "DT", 1.0, -1.2, "T"), D("T2", "DT", 1.0, 2.0, "T"),
       D("E2", "DE", 1.0, 5.8, "E"), D("M", "MIKE", 5.0, 0.8, "M"), D("D1", "NB", 6.0, 11.5, "$"),
       D("D2", "DB", 6.0, 7.5, "D"), D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -15.0, "C"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.5, 17.0, "C"),
       D("FS", "FS", 13.0, -6.0, "FS"), D("SS", "SS", 13.0, 9.0, "SS")]
pt = Play(off, dfn, los=45, to_go=8)
pt.highlight("RB", color=WATCH)
pt.highlight("Y", color=TE_RING)
fld = pt.draw(lateral=(-19, 21), window=(-7, 14.6), title=False)
no_numbers(fld.ax)
plt.show()
```

**Run or pass? Who on the offense is likely to touch the ball, and what kind of fantasy player is B?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**A pass, very likely, and B is the passing-down back.** The situation alone makes it a pass: third-and-8 is a
passing down at any score, and in 2025 teams trailing by 9 to 15 points in the fourth quarter threw on about
four plays in five even before you add the down and distance. The personnel agree: three receivers to one side,
the quarterback in the gun, and the defense in [dime](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-dime), expecting a throw.

The back on the field tells you about usage. The team swapped its early-down runner, A, for B, a back it trusts
to pick up a blitzer and run a route, which is why B is on the field when the team must throw. Expect B to stay
in to block if the defense shows pressure, and to release to the flat or over the middle as a
[checkdown](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-checkdown) if it doesn't. The slot receivers, H and the detached
tight end Y, are the other likely targets on a throw aimed just past the
[line to gain](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-line-to-gain). And if the offense does run, it will be a
[draw](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-draw) to B: with only five defenders in the box, a draw against dime is
the one run coordinators like on third-and-long, and it's another reason B rather than A is out there.

For fantasy, B is the classic PPR back: few carries, but targets in exactly the game scripts where his team
trails. In standard scoring he is barely worth a roster spot; in PPR, on a team that trails often, he can be a
weekly starter, the 2025 Kenny Gainwell profile. A, meanwhile, is a game-script player: valuable when his team
leads, invisible when it doesn't.
:::
:::

## Takeaways

- **Fantasy points are outputs; usage is the input the scheme controls.** Opportunity statistics (target
  share, air-yards share, WOPR, route participation) repeat from season to season far better than efficiency,
  and touchdowns barely repeat at all.
- **Read receivers in order: on the field, running a route, targeted, targeted deep, productive per route.**
  Snap share hides blocking snaps; route participation and YPRR fix that, and a productive part-timer whose
  role grows is the cheapest upside in fantasy.
- **A running back's touchdowns belong to whoever has the goal-line job.** Snap share and carries describe the
  role between the 20s; red-zone share, and especially who gets the ball inside the 5 and the 2, decides the
  scoring. In 12 personnel the tight end is a receiver only if he runs routes.
- **Volume = plays × pass rate × target rate × share.** PROE sets the team's taste and moves volume, not a
  number one's share; pace adds or subtracts plays for everyone; game script overrides both late in games, and
  the betting lines forecast it (a big favorite's extra plays are runs and touchdowns).
- **Know the format and the price.** PPR rewards catches and lifts pass-catching backs and slot receivers.
  ADP is a market price set by points above replacement, which is why fantasy running backs are dear when NFL
  ones are cheap; value is beating that price, most often by spotting a usage change the box score hasn't shown.
- **When the play-caller changes, his fingerprint travels; his old stars don't.** Check who calls plays and what
  the head coach wants, what his last offense did and how much of it was its players, and what roster he
  inherited; name a loser as well as a winner; then verify with a month of data, trusting every-play rates
  sooner than shares.

the [Shanahan tree](../12-case-studies/12-03-shanahan-wide-zone-tree.qmd) (McDaniel's motion and wide zone), the
[Chiefs](../12-case-studies/12-04-reid-chiefs.qmd) (Reid's play-calling across three coordinators) and the
[Lions](../12-case-studies/12-07-lions-ben-johnson-and-campbell.qmd) (the offense Petzing inherits).

::: {.callout-note title="Go deeper"}
Josh Hermsmeyer's air-yards work (archived at FiveThirtyEight and in his later writing) is the foundation of
WOPR, RACR (receiver air conversion ratio: receiving yards per air yard thrown his way) and the habit of reading
opportunity before production. The nflverse data dictionary documents the
`target_share`, `air_yards_share` and `wopr` columns that `load_player_stats()` computes for every player and
week, and nflverse's `load_ff_opportunity()` adds expected fantasy points built from usage (each carry and
target valued by where it happened), which is this chapter's idea turned into a model. For route-level data,
PFF and FTN chart routes run by every player; snap counts are free through `load_snap_counts()`, and betting
lines for every game sit in nflverse's schedules (`spread_line`, `total_line`). To extend the chapter's charts, change the season in the data
cell, or swap the `neutral()` filter for your own definition and watch how the PROE ranking moves.
:::

[^data]: Course calculation from nflverse regular-season play-by-play (2024-2025) and `load_participation()`
(FTN-sourced for both seasons): wide receivers and tight ends with 50 or more targets in both seasons (n = 78);
for a player with two teams in a season, the team where he drew more targets. Target share and air-yards share
are measured against the team's totals in the games the player was on the field; two-point tries excluded.
"Route participation (est.)" is the share of the team's dropbacks (`qb_dropback == 1`, which includes sacks
and scrambles) on which the player was listed on the field, and "yards per route run (est.)" divides
receiving yards by those dropbacks; true route counts come from PFF or FTN film charting and are lower for
anyone who sometimes blocks.

[^wopr]: The formula as implemented in nflverse: "wopr: Weighted Opportunity Rating, 1.5 × target_share +
0.7 × air_yards_share," nflreadr data dictionary, player stats: https://nflreadr.nflverse.com/articles/dictionary_player_stats.html .
Hermsmeyer as its creator, alongside RACR and PACR: Action Network, "WOPR" explainer: https://www.actionnetwork.com/article/p/601206703 ;
Dynasty Nerds, https://www.dynastynerds.com/?p=33320 ; 4for4 author page ("creator of airyards.com and Air Yards
based metrics PACR, RACR and WOPR"): https://www.4for4.com/users/josh-hermsmeyer/author-page . Hermsmeyer's
original airyards.com write-up is no longer online; the weights here are the ones every secondary source and
nflverse use.

[^adp]: FanDuel Research, "Fantasy Football: It's Never Been Easier to Draft Saquon Barkley" (July 2024):
https://www.fanduel.com/research/fantasy-football-it-s-never-been-easier-to-draft-saquon-barkley (FantasyPros
consensus half-PPR ADP, pick 17 and RB6, "his lowest ADP in seven seasons," i.e. of his career; the article
uses July 2024 ADP data). ADP kept moving in August, so treat 17 as the July price.

[^barkley]: Course calculation from nflverse 2024 regular-season play-by-play and `load_player_stats()`:
345 carries, 2,005 yards, 13 rushing touchdowns in 16 games; 33 catches on 43 targets for 278 yards and 2
touchdowns; 58% of the Eagles' runs (scrambles included); 322.3 standard and 355.3 PPR fantasy points
(first and second among running backs). Eagles' neutral PROE −8.8, third-lowest. Snap share: Pro Football
Reference snap counts via nflverse, 73% average. Inside the 2-yard line: Hurts 18 carries or targets and 11
touchdowns, Barkley 6 and 2. Pro Football Reference: https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/B/BarkSa00.htm .
Week 18: Nick Sirianni announced that Barkley and other starters would sit against the Giants with Philadelphia
locked into the No. 2 seed (Detroit and Minnesota were playing for No. 1), leaving him 100 yards short of Eric
Dickerson's record: NBC Sports Philadelphia, https://www.nbcsportsphiladelphia.com/nfl/philadelphia-eagles/eagles-inactives-saquon-barkley-officially-inactive-nfl-week-18/640273 ;
SI, https://www.si.com/nfl/eagles/onsi/news/eagles-saquon-barkley-gets-honest-about-sitting-week-18-pat3 .

[^heavy]: 12 personnel share: course calculation from nflverse participation data, regular-season pass and run
plays (see Personnel Groupings). Fewer than three wide receivers: NFL Next Gen Stats via NFL.com, "NFL trend
watch: Heavy personnel could shape Super Bowl LX showdown between Patriots and Seahawks":
https://www.nfl.com/news/nfl-trend-watch-heavy-personnel-could-shape-super-bowl-lx-showdown-between-patriots-and-seahawks .

[^goppl]: "Fantasy football (gridiron)," Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fantasy_football_(gridiron) ,
on Wilfred "Bill" Winkenbach and the GOPPPL, whose rules were worked out in 1962 at a New York hotel during a
Raiders road trip, with a first draft in August 1963; NFL.com, "Let's play GOPPL: Digging out the roots of fantasy
football": https://www.nfl.com/news/let-s-play-goppl-digging-out-the-roots-of-fantasy-football-09000d5d80874333 .
The original scoring paid only for touchdowns (rushing, receiving or passing), field goals, extra points and return
touchdowns; yardage came later.

[^ppr]: RotoWire, "What is PPR in fantasy football?": https://www.rotowire.com/football/article/what-is-ppr-in-fantasy-football-94969 ;
Sports Illustrated, "Fantasy Football 101: What Are PPR (Point Per Reception) Leagues?":
https://www.si.com/fantasy/fantasy-football-101-what-are-ppr-point-per-reception-leagues-01k0y4hz2k7n .
The 2000s spread: the high-stakes NFFC adopted PPR at its founding in 2004 (founder Greg Ambrosius,
NFFC forums: https://nffcforums.shgn.com/viewtopic.php?p=46813 ), and Footballguys added PPR scoring and
rankings in 2008 (https://www.footballguys.com/article/Pasquino_Points_Per_Deception_2014 ). Site defaults:
"ESPN's default is full-point PPR, Yahoo's is .5 PPR," RotoWire: https://www.rotowire.com/football/article/weekly-rankings-41764 .
